ety.text: Late Middle English, of North Germanic origin, from West Old Norse raptr, from Proto-Germanic *raf-tra-, from Proto-Indo-European *rap-tro-, from *rep- (“stake, beam”). See also Norwegian raft (“beam, rafter”), Danish raft (“thin pole”). Compare also Albanian trap (“raft, ferry”).

senses.d: A flat-bottomed craft able to float and drift on water, used for transport or as a waterborne platform.
ex: They floated down the river on an inflatable raft

senses.d: Any flattish thing, usually wooden, used in a similar fashion.
A thick crowd of aquatic birds, particularly a group floating on the surface of the water.
ex: Pelicans, bills stuck forward, would gather in small rafts to move along in comical formation, before diving in unison […]
Occasionally, there was a large black raft of birds far out at sea.

senses.d: A group of aquatic mammals, especially otters and especially when visible on the surface of the water.
ex: A raft of otters at rest in the river.
News of Smith's discovery of the South Shetland Islands, and of the rafts of seals along their shores, spread quickly.

senses.d: A group of alligators or crocodiles, especially when floating in water with their backs visible above the surface.
ex: She even pointed out a bank where a raft of crocodiles lay dozing, baking their scaly backs in the sun.
navigation was obstructed by a raft of alligators

senses.d: A collection of logs, fallen trees, etc. which obstructs navigation in a river.
A square array of sensors forming part of a large telescope.
A mass of congealed solids that forms on a consommé because of the protein in the egg white.
To dock (toolbars, etc.) so that they share horizontal or vertical space.
ex: The ToolStripContainer provides built-in rafting and docking of ToolStrip, MenuStrip, and StatusStrip controls.

senses.d: A large (but unspecified) number, a lot.

grp.label: large but unspecified number of something

ety.text: Borrowed from Old Occitan radel, a diminutive of rat, itself from Latin ratis (“raft”).

it:zattera.gl: raft (primitive vessel, modern emergency or sports craft)

ety.text: From zatta, ultimately of Germanic origin. Alternatively, from Lombardic zattera, from Proto-West Germanic *tat(t)ur.
From Paleo-Hispanic, probably Basque [Term?] or Iberian [Term?].
Paleo-Hispanicder. Spanish balsabor. Portuguese balsa Borrowed from Spanish balsa.
Borrowed from Malayalam ചങ്ങാടം (caṅṅāṭaṁ), from Sanskrit संघाट (saṃghāṭa).
From Latin massa, from Ancient Greek μᾶζα (mâza, “bread”).
Borrowed from Latin multitūdinem, with the change of the ending to -tud. Compare the inherited doublet muchedumbre. Compare Portuguese multidão.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin multitudinem. Doublet of multitude.

phr: Adam and Eve on a raft
